newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Greens join forces for election.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Greens join forces for election.

text.p: The opposition Socialists and the tiny Greens party agreed on Wednesday to field more than 100 joint candidates for France's snap parliamentary election.

"For the first time in their history, the Greens will be able to enter the National Assembly," Greens leader Dominique Voynet predicted at a joint news conference with Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin ahead of the May 25-June 1 vote called by the centre-right government.

Under the deal, Greens candidates would represent the Socialists in 29 constituencies while Socialist candidates in 77 constituencies would also represent the Greens and the tiny Radical party. The National Assembly has 577 seats.
Elsewhere, the parties would fight on rival platforms.
"This is an innovation," Jospin said. "The ecologists and the Socialists are agreed on broad targets and on presenting joint candidates."

Voynet, a doctor and a single mother who won 3.3 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election won by Gaullist Jacques Chirac, will be the unity candidate in Dole in the Jura. She is among the Greens with the best chances of winning a seat.
The left is seeking to overturn opinion polls showing that Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right coalition is likely to retain power in the election though with a smaller majority.
The joint candidacies will give the Socialists a head start on the horse trading which normally takes place before the second round run-off votes in seats where no one wins a first round majority.
The Communist Party and the tiny Citizens' Movement, which has four seats in parliament, also agreed on Wednesday to joint candidacies in 44 constituencies -- 30 Communists and 14 from the MDC.

Communist leader Robert Hue and MDC leader Jean-Pierre Chevenement, a former Socialist defence minister, accused the government of preparing a new bout of austerity and creating an "ultraliberal and fundamentally unequal model of society".
Both Hue and Chevenement oppose the Maastricht Treaty and the single European currency, the euro.

On Tuesday, Jospin and Hue agreed an electoral pact, calling for job creation and cuts in working hours but papering over wide cracks on Europe -- Jospin favours the euro on certain conditions. The Socialist-Communist deal stops well short of fielding joint candidates.
Meanwhile, France's three main labour unions, often bitterly at odds, called for a unity march in Paris on May 1 for the first time in 14 years to denounce unemployment and racism.

But the march underscored their differences. It was backed by the national leadership of the pro-Socialist CFDT and the Communist-led CGT but merely by the Paris branch of the independent Force Ouvriere (FO).

FO leader Marc Blondel, who planned to march instead in the southwestern city of Bordeaux, said the planned march was "more to do with politics than unions" and said he did not share the views of either the CGT or the CFDT.
The FO and the CGT spearheaded a crippling 24-day wave of strikes in late 1995, mainly triggered by health care reforms.

A CSA opinion poll predicted on Tuesday the centre-right would retain a majority with 296 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France, ahead of the Socialists on 237, the Communists on 21 and the far-right National Front on one.
Most of the other 22 constituencies, in French overseas territories ranging from the Pacific to the Caribbean, are held by the centre-right.
